name: Visual Rhythm and Scaling Hierarchy — Multi-Scale Periodic Prediction in Architectural Pattern
short_description: Repeating architectural elements create visual rhythm during scanning; scaling hierarchies provide structure at every scale; visual nourishment vs. visual starvation
structural_pattern: Architecture presents visual information at multiple spatial scales simultaneously: building massing (10–100m), facade articulation (1–10m), window/column rhythm (0.5–3m), ornamental detail (0.01–0.5m), and material grain (0.001–0.01m, addressed by T1). At each scale, repeating elements (columns, arches, windows, cornice brackets, ornamental modules) create PERIODIC visual structure that the visual system processes as rhythm — analogous to the auditory temporal prediction in music. Visual scanning of a facade produces a temporal sequence of prediction-and-confirmation events. Regular spacing → strong period prediction → low PE → processing fluency. Variation within regularity → moderate PE → visual interest. Random placement → no periodic prediction possible → high PE → visual fatigue. SCALING HIERARCHY (Salingaros): buildings with structure at EVERY scale engage the visual prediction system at multiple frequencies simultaneously — 'visual nourishment.' Buildings missing intermediate scales produce 'visual starvation.'
higher_order_principle: Multi-scale visual prediction as the visual instantiation of the general principle that the brain prefers moderate PE at multiple levels simultaneously. T1 (fractal fluency) captures the STATISTICAL structure of visual complexity (1/f spectral profile). VF2 captures the PERIODIC structure of visual complexity (spatial frequency content from repeating elements). Together, T1 + VF2 describe the full visual prediction landscape: T1 for the aperiodic, self-similar component; VF2 for the periodic, rhythmic component.

musical_analogy.eye_scanning_motion: Temporal performance of the visual score

causal_links.evidence_base: Repeating architectural elements create spatial periodicity that the visual system detects and predicts. Supported by visual statistical learning literature (Fiser & Aslin, 2001, ~1,500 citations) and visual rhythm perception. Architectural-specific quantification by Salingaros (2005) and Taylor et al. (2005).

Buildings with structure at every scale (complete scaling hierarchy) engage visual processing at all spatial frequencies → 'visual nourishment.' Buildings missing intermediate scales → 'visual starvation' at those frequencies. Salingaros (2005) articulates the principle; empirical parameterization is limited.

Regular rhythm → low PE → fluency. Moderate variation → moderate PE → engagement ('visual groove'). Random or absent rhythm → high PE or no PE → fatigue or blankness. Parallels M9 groove Goldilocks zone. Architectural-specific evidence limited.

scope_conditions: Applies to building facades, interior surfaces, urban streetscapes, and any architectural element with repeating structure
Visual rhythm is experienced during SCANNING — it requires the eye to move across the pattern. Static fixation does not produce rhythmic prediction
Scale-dependence: the relevant scale depends on viewing distance. A facade rhythm visible from 50m may be invisible from 500m; ornamental detail visible from 2m disappears at 20m
Photography vs. in-person: photographs compress the scaling hierarchy by fixing the viewing distance. In-person experience allows the viewer to engage different scales by approaching or retreating
moderators: Viewing distance: determines which scales are visible and therefore which levels of the hierarchy are engaged
Movement speed: pedestrians engage more scales than drivers; slow movement reveals more detail
Lighting: raking light reveals surface detail (connecting to L1 and MAT3); flat light flattens the hierarchy
Cultural familiarity: repeated exposure to a visual vocabulary (Classical, Gothic, Islamic) strengthens period prediction for that vocabulary

interactions.nature: T1 captures aperiodic fractal structure. VF2 captures periodic rhythmic structure. Together they describe the full visual complexity profile.
VF2 contributes to overall visual complexity assessed by T2. Multi-scale engagement with moderate PE at each scale IS the condition for T2's Goldilocks zone.
VF1 describes the shape of repeating elements. VF2 describes their spatial arrangement. A colonnade has both VF1 properties (column contour) and VF2 properties (column spacing rhythm).
